paragraphs: CHAPTER ONE
“Without a house—without a home—without hope!”

Many who had walked that street before him must have said the same: the weary, the lonely, the hungry, the abandoned, all the lost and struggling people forever coming and going along the pavements of Lambeth Parish, cold, starving and miserable. But it is doubtful whether anyone had spoken with a firmer conviction that the words were true, or with sharper self-pity, than the young man hurrying along Vauxhall Walk one rainy winter night, with neither an overcoat on his shoulders nor a hat on his head.

It was a strange thing for a man of twenty-one to say, stranger still from someone who looked like a gentleman and was one. Fortune did not appear to have treated him particularly badly. Nothing about him would have made a passer-by imagine he had been defeated in a long struggle against disaster. His boots were neither worn down at the heels nor split at the toes, like so many, many that dragged, shuffled and scraped along the pavement. His clothes were good and fashionable, without the tears, patches and rags of the people slinking miserably past, crouching in doorways, or silently holding out a hand for charity. Hunger had not pinched his face; wickedness had not lined it, nor drink and wild excess brutalised it. Yet he said and believed he had no hope, and in his youthful despair almost spoke the words aloud.

It was a bad night to be outside with such feelings. The rain was cold, merciless and growing heavier. A sharp, damp wind blew down the side streets from the river. The fumes from the gasworks seemed to fall with the rain. The road was muddy, the pavement greasy and slippery, and the lamps burnt dimly. That dreary district of London looked at its bleakest and worst.

Certainly, it was no evening to be out without a home to go to or sixpence in one’s pocket. Yet that was exactly the situation of the young gentleman striding bareheaded along Vauxhall Walk, with rain beating on his unprotected head.

He looked enviously at the large, fine houses. Once prosperous citizens had lived in them; now most were let a floor at a time to weekly tenants. He would have given much for a room, or even part of one. He had been walking a long time—since dark, in fact, and darkness comes early in December. He was tired, cold and hungry, with nothing to look forward to but walking the streets all night.

As he passed a lamp, its light showed a handsome young face and an expressive, sensitive mouth. His eyebrows had that particular shape—not quite a frown, but a certain drawing together—often taken as a sign of genius. More reliably, it goes with an impulsive nature, easily pleased and easily depressed, capable of keen suffering or intense enjoyment. In his short life he had enjoyed little and suffered a good deal. That night, walking bareheaded through the rain, he had reached a crisis.
As far as he could see or reason in his despair, the best thing he could do was die. The world did not want him. He would be better out of it.

One house had its front door open. In the dimly lit hall he could see a few pieces of furniture waiting to be taken away. A van stood beside the kerb. As he paused for a second, two men were lifting a table into it.

“Ah,” he thought, “even those poor people have somewhere to go, some shelter waiting. I haven’t a roof over my head or a shilling for a night’s lodging.” He hurried on as though driven by memory, so fast that a man running after him struggled to catch up.
“Master Graham! Master Graham!” the man called breathlessly. Hearing himself addressed, the young man stopped as suddenly as if he had been shot.
“Who are you? How do you know me?” he asked, turning round.
“I’m William. Don’t you remember William, Master Graham? And for the Lord’s sake, sir, what are you doing out on a night like this without your hat?”
“I forgot it,” he answered, “and I didn’t care to go back for it.”
“Then why not buy another, sir? You’ll catch your death of cold. Besides, forgive me, sir, but it does look strange.”
“I know,” Master Graham said grimly, “but I haven’t a halfpenny in the world.”
“Have you and the master, then—” the man began, but hesitated and stopped.
“Had a quarrel? Yes, one that will last us our whole lives,” the other finished with a bitter laugh.
“And where are you going now?”
“Going? Nowhere, except to find the softest paving stone or the shelter of an arch.”
“You’re joking, sir.”
“I don’t feel much like joking either.”
“Will you come back with me, Master Graham? We’re almost finished moving, but there’s still a spark of fire in the grate. We could talk better out of this rain. Will you come, sir?”
“Come? Of course I will,” said the young man. They turned and walked back to the house he had looked into as he passed.

It was an old, old house, with a long, broad hall and shallow stairs that were easy to climb. Deep cornices bordered the ceilings; the floors were oak and the doors mahogany. All still spoke silently of the wealth and solid standing of the original owner. He had lived before anyone thought of the Tradescants or Ashmoles, and had slept far longer than they in St Mary’s churchyard, near the archbishop’s palace.
“Come upstairs, sir,” urged the departing tenant. “It’s cold down here with the door wide open.”
“Did you have the whole house, then, William?” Graham Coulton asked in surprise.

“All of it. And I, for one, am very sorry to leave. But nothing else would satisfy my wife. This room, sir.” With a little visible pride in showing his former home, William invited his guest into a spacious first-floor room stretching the full width of the house.
Tired though he was, the young man could not hold back an exclamation of surprise.
“Why, we have nothing this large at home, William,” he said.
“It’s a fine house,” William answered, raking the embers together and throwing wood on them. “But, like many a good family, it has fallen on hard times.”

The room had four windows, tightly shuttered, with deep, low window seats. They suggested pleasant days long past, when cushions and curtains had made cosy retreats for children and sometimes adults too. No furniture remained, unless you counted an oak bench with a high back beside the hearth, a large mirror set into the panelling at the far end, and the black marble wall table beneath it. Yet the absence of chairs and tables showed the room’s magnificent proportions to their full advantage. Nothing distracted from the decorated ceiling, the panelled walls, the old-fashioned mantelpiece with its curious carvings, or the tiled fireplace. Each tile held a picture of a biblical or allegorical subject.
“If you were staying here, William,” Coulton said, dropping wearily onto the bench, “I’d ask you to let me spend the night where I am.”

“If you can make do, sir, I don’t know of anything to stop you staying,” the man answered, fanning the wood into flame. “I won’t return the key to the landlord until tomorrow. At any rate, this would be better than the cold streets.”
“Do you really mean it?” the other asked eagerly. “I’d be grateful to lie here. I’m completely exhausted.”

“Then stay, Master Graham. You’re welcome. I’ll fetch a basket of coal I was going to put in the van and build a good fire for you to warm yourself. Then I must run round to the other house for a minute or two. It isn’t far, and I’ll be back as soon as I can.”
“Thank you, William. You’ve always been good to me,” the young man said gratefully. “This is delightful.” He stretched his numb hands over the blazing wood and looked round with a satisfied smile.

“I never expected to find accommodation like this,” he remarked as his friend in need returned, carrying a half-bushel basket full of coal and using it to build a roaring fire. “The last thing I imagined was meeting someone I knew in Vauxhall Walk.”
“Where had you come from, Master Graham?” William asked curiously.

“Old Melfield’s. I used to go to his school, you know. Now he’s retired and lives in Kennington Oval on the proceeds of years of robbery. I thought he might lend me a pound, offer me a bed for the night, or even a glass of wine. But oh dear, no. He took the moral high ground and said he could have nothing to do with a son who defied his father’s authority.
“He gave me plenty of advice and nothing else, then showed me out into the rain with such smooth politeness that I could have struck him.”
William muttered something that was not a blessing, then said aloud:
“At any rate, I think you’re better here, sir. I’ll be back in less than half an hour.”

Alone, young Coulton took off his coat. He moved the bench a little and hung the coat over its end to dry. He rubbed some of the water from his hair with his handkerchief. Then, utterly exhausted, he lay down before the fire, rested his head on his arm and fell fast asleep.

Nearly an hour later, he woke to the sound of someone gently tending the fire and moving quietly around the room. He sat up suddenly and looked round, confused for a moment. Then he recognised his humble friend and said with a laugh:
“I’d completely lost myself. I couldn’t imagine where I was.”
“I’m sorry to see you here, sir,” came the reply, “but it’s better than being outdoors. It’s turned into a nasty night. I’ve brought a blanket you might like to wrap yourself in.”
“I wish you’d brought something to eat as well,” the young man said, laughing.
“Are you hungry, sir?” William asked with concern.

“Yes. I’ve eaten nothing since breakfast. My father and I began quarrelling the moment we sat down to lunch, and I got up and left the table. But hunger doesn’t matter. I’m dry and warm, and I can forget the rest by sleeping.”
“It’s too late to buy anything now,” the man said to himself. “The shops closed long ago.
“Do you think, sir,” he added, brightening, “you could manage some bread and cheese?”
“Do I think? I’d call it a perfect feast,” Graham Coulton answered. “But don’t worry about food tonight, William. You’ve had more than enough trouble already.”
William’s only answer was to hurry to the door and run downstairs. Soon he returned with bread and cheese wrapped in paper in one hand and a pewter measure full of beer in the other.
“It’s the best I could do, sir,” he said apologetically. “I had to beg it from the landlady.”
“Here’s to her health!” the young man cried cheerfully, taking a long drink from the tankard. “That tastes better than champagne in my father’s house.”
“Won’t he be worried about you?” William ventured. He had emptied the coal basket and now sat on it upside down, watching wistfully as his former master’s son ate the bread and cheese with relish.
“No,” came the firm answer. “When he hears it pouring, he’ll only hope I’m outside in the downpour. He’ll say a good soaking will cool my pride.”
“I don’t think you’re right about that,” the man remarked.
“But I’m certain. My father has always hated me, just as he hated my mother.”
“Forgive me, sir, but he loved your mother too much.”
“If you’d heard what he said about her today, you might change your opinion. He said I was like her in mind as well as body: a coward, a fool and a hypocrite.”
“He didn’t mean it, sir.”
“He meant every word. He does think I’m a coward, because I—I—” The young man broke into a fit of hysterical tears.

“I don’t much like leaving you here alone,” William said, glancing round with a sudden troubled look. “But I have nowhere suitable to ask you to stay, and I must leave. I’m a night watchman, and I have to be on duty at twelve.”
“I’ll be all right,” he answered. “I just mustn’t talk any more about my father. Tell me about yourself, William. How did you get such a big house, and why are you leaving?”
“The landlord put me in charge, sir. My wife took it into her head not to like the place.”
“Why didn’t she like it?”

“She felt desperately lonely, alone here with the children at night,” William answered, turning his head away. A moment later he added, “Now, sir, if there’s nothing else I can do for you, I’d better go.
“It’s getting late. I’ll come round tomorrow morning.”
“Goodnight,” the young man said, holding out his hand. William took it as openly and freely as it was offered. “What would I have done tonight if I hadn’t happened to meet you?”
“I don’t believe much happens by chance in this world, Master Graham,” came the quiet answer. “I do hope you rest well and don’t suffer for getting so wet.”
“No fear of that,” he replied. A moment later, the young man was alone in the Old House in Vauxhall Walk.
CHAPTER TWO

Lying on the bench, with the fire burnt out and the room completely dark, Graham Coulton had a strange dream. He thought he woke from a deep sleep to find a log smouldering on the hearth and the mirror at the far end of the room reflecting flickers of light.
He could not understand how, so far from the mirror, he could see everything in it. But he accepted the difficulty without surprise, as people generally do in dreams.
Nor was he surprised to see the outline of a woman sitting beside the fire, picking something up from her lap and dropping it with a despairing gesture.

He heard the soft ring of gold and knew she was lifting and dropping sovereigns. He turned a little to look at the person occupied in this strange, pointless way. Where there had been no chair the night before, there was one now. On it sat an old, wrinkled hag in poor, ragged clothes. A soft cap barely covered her thin white hair. Her cheeks were sunken, her nose hooked, and her fingers looked more like talons than anything else. They plunged into the heap of gold, lifting handfuls only to scatter them mournfully.
“Oh, my lost life!” she moaned in a voice of bitter anguish. “Oh, my lost life! If only I could have one day, one hour of it again!”

Out of the darkness, out of the corner where the shadows were deepest, out of the gloom by the door, out of the dreary night, came old men and young children, worn-out women and weary hearts. Their feet were soaked; water dripped from their heads. That gold could have relieved their misery, but instead it mocked their wretchedness.

Around the miser, who had once sat gloating where she now sat lamenting, crowded all those pale, sad figures: the very old, the baby only hours old, the sobbing outcast, the honest poor and the repentant sinner. From their pale lips came just one low cry: a plea for the help she could have given but had withheld.

Together they gathered close, as each had done alone during life. They prayed, sobbed and begged. With haggard eyes, the figure looked at the poor she had turned away, the children whose cries she had refused to hear, and the old people she had let starve and die for want of what would have been a mere trifle to her. Then, with a terrible scream, she lifted her thin arms above her head and sank down—down. Gold scattered from her lap and rolled across the floor until its gleam vanished into the darkness beyond.

Then Graham Coulton woke in earnest, sweat seeping from every pore. He felt a fear and agony unlike anything he had ever known, and the heartbreaking cry of “Oh, my lost life!” still rang in his ears.
There also seemed to have been some lesson for him mixed up in it all, but he had forgotten it. However hard he tried, he could not remember what had slipped away at the very moment he woke.
He lay thinking about it for a little while. Then, still heavy with sleep, he made his way back into dreams.

Perhaps it was natural that the earlier vision should return among the strange fantasies of night and darkness. Before long, the young man found himself struggling through scene after scene in which the woman he had seen beside the dying fire played the chief part.

He saw her walking slowly across the floor, chewing a dry crust—this woman who could have bought every luxury wealth could command. On the hearth stood a man with a commanding presence, dressed in the fashion of long ago, watching her. Dark anger filled his eyes, and disgust curled his lips into a smile. Somehow, even asleep, the dreamer understood that he was seeing an ancestor looking at his descendant. The house, now serving such humble purposes, had never fallen as far from its former greatness as this woman with her pitiful soul. She was infected with the most contemptible and insidious vice humanity knows. Every other vice seems connected with the flesh, but a miser’s greed eats into the soul itself.

Filthy, repulsive and hard-hearted though she was, he saw another phantom enter and meet her almost at the doorway. It took her hand and seemed to plead for help. He could not hear everything, but caught a word here and there: talk of former days, mention of a beautiful young mother, an appeal, it seemed, to the time when they had been a little brother and sister, before the cursed greed for gold divided them. All in vain. The hag answered him just as she had answered the children, young girls and old people in the earlier vision. Family affection could not reach her heart any more than human sympathy had. He seemed to be begging for help to avert some cruel misfortune or terrible disgrace. The hardest stone might have yielded more readily to his plea. Then the figure on the hearth changed into an angel, which sorrowfully folded its wings over its face. The man slowly left the room with his head bowed.

As he left, the scene changed again. It was night, and the miser was making her way upstairs. Graham Coulton imagined he watched from below as she struggled wearily from step to step. She had aged strangely since the earlier scenes. She moved with difficulty; each step seemed to demand an enormous effort. Her skinny hand passed along the banisters with slow, painful care. Fascinated, the young man watched the progress of that frail, decrepit woman. Alone in a desolate house, she faced a blackness deeper than night, waiting to swallow her.

After that, Graham Coulton seemed to lie for a while in quiet, dreamless sleep. On waking, he found himself entering a bedroom whose furnishings were as shabby and filthy as the woman in his earlier vision. The poorest labourer’s wife would have surrounded herself with more comforts than this room held. At first, in the dim light so often found in dreams, he could make out only a four-poster bed without any curtains, a crookedly raised blind, an old carpet covered in dust, dirt on the floor, a shaky washstand with all its paint worn off, an old mahogany dressing table, and a cracked mirror speckled all over.
Gradually, he made out the shape of someone huddled on the bed. Moving closer, he saw it was the woman whose dreadful presence seemed to fill the house.

What a terrible sight she was. Thin white hair lay scattered over the pillow, and scraps of blankets were gathered around her shoulders. Her claw-like fingers clutched the bedclothes as though she guarded her gold even in sleep.
It was an awful, repulsive sight, but not half as terrifying as what followed.
As the young man watched, he heard stealthy footsteps on the stairs. First one man, then another, crept cautiously into the room. A second later, both stood beside the bed with murder in their eyes.

Graham Coulton tried to shout and tried to move. But the strange power that holds us helpless in dreams tied his tongue and paralysed his limbs. He could only watch and listen. Suddenly awakened, the woman started up, only to be struck by one of the ruffians. The other followed by plunging a knife into her breast.
With a gurgling scream, she fell back on the bed. At that same moment Graham Coulton cried out and woke again, thanking heaven it was only an illusion.
CHAPTER THREE
“I hope you slept well, sir.” It was William, entering the hall with the sunlight of a fine, bright morning streaming in behind him. “Did you have a good night’s rest?”
Graham Coulton laughed and answered:

“Well, honestly, I was rather like Paddy, ‘who couldn’t sleep for dreaming’. I suppose I slept well enough. But whether it was the quarrel with my father, the hard bed or the cheese—most likely the bread and cheese so late at night—I had the most extraordinary dreams all night long. Some old woman kept appearing, and I saw her murdered.”
“Surely not, sir?” William said nervously.
“Yes, indeed,” he replied. “But that’s all over now. I’ve been down to the kitchen for a good wash, and I’m fresh as a daisy and hungry as a hunter. Oh, William, can you get me some breakfast?”
“Certainly, Master Graham. I’ve brought a kettle, and I’ll boil the water straight away. I suppose, sir”—he asked this cautiously—“you’ll be going home today?”

“Home?” the young man repeated. “Certainly not. I’ll never go home until I return with a medal on my coat, or a leg or arm cut off. I’ve thought it all through, William. I’ll enlist. There’s talk of war. Whether I live or die, my father will have reason to take back his belief that I’m a coward.”
“I’m sure the Admiral never thought anything of the kind, sir,” William said. “Why, you have the courage of ten men!”
“Not in front of him,” the young man answered sadly.
“You won’t do anything rash, Master Graham? You won’t enlist, or do anything like that, in anger?”
“If I don’t, what will become of me?” he asked. “I can’t dig, and I’m ashamed to beg.
“Why, without you, I wouldn’t even have had a roof over my head last night.”
“Not much of a roof, I’m afraid, sir.”

“Not much of a roof?” the young man repeated. “Who could want a better one? What an excellent room this is.” He looked round the room, where William was lighting a fire. “You could easily give dinner to twenty people here.”
“If you think so highly of it, Master Graham, you might stay a while, until you decide what to do. I’m quite sure the landlord won’t object.”
“Oh, nonsense. He’d want a high rent for a house like this.”
“I expect he would, if he could get it,” William answered meaningfully.
“What do you mean? Can’t he let the place?”
“No, sir. I didn’t tell you last night, but there was a murder here. People have been wary of the house ever since.”
“A murder? What sort of murder? Who was killed?”

“A woman, Master Graham—the landlord’s sister. She lived here all alone and was supposed to have money. Whether she did or not, she was found dead with a stab wound in her breast. If there was any money, it must have been stolen at the same time. None has ever been found in the house, from that day to this.”
“Was that why your wife wouldn’t stay?” the young man asked, leaning against the mantelpiece and looking thoughtfully down at William.

“Yes, sir. She couldn’t bear it any longer. She became thinner and more nervous than you’d believe. She never saw anything, but she said she heard footsteps and voices. Whenever she walked through the hall or up the stairs, she felt someone was following her. We put the children to bed in that big room you had last night, and they said they often saw an old woman sitting by the hearth. Nothing ever came my way,” William finished with a laugh. “I was always ready to sleep the moment my head touched the pillow.”
“Were the murderers never found?” Graham Coulton asked.

“No, sir. The landlord, Miss Tynan’s brother, has always been suspected—quite wrongly, I’m sure. But he’ll never clear his name now. People knew he’d come to ask her for help a day or two before the murder. They also knew that within a week or two he’d managed to get through whatever trouble had been worrying him. Then, you see, the money was never found. Altogether, people hardly knew what to think.”
“Humph!” Graham Coulton said, pacing up and down the room a few times.
“Could I go and see this landlord?”
“Certainly, sir, if you had a hat,” William answered with such solemn politeness that the young man burst out laughing.
“That is certainly an obstacle,” he remarked. “A note will have to do instead. I have a pencil in my pocket, so here goes.”
Within half an hour of sending the note, William returned with a sovereign and the landlord’s compliments. He would be much obliged if Mr Coulton could “come round”.
“You won’t do anything rash, sir?” William pleaded.
“Why, man,” the young fellow answered, “I might as well be killed by a ghost as a bullet.
“What is there to be afraid of?”

William only shook his head. He did not think his young master had it in him to stay alone in a haunted house and solve the mystery it certainly held entirely by his own efforts. Yet when Graham Coulton left the landlord’s house, he looked brighter and more cheerful than usual. He walked along the Lambeth road towards the place where William was waiting, humming a tune as he went.
“We’ve settled it,” he said. “Now, if my father wants his son for Christmas, he’ll have a hard time finding him.”
“Don’t say that, Master Graham, don’t,” the man begged with a shiver. “Perhaps it would have been better, after all, if you’d never happened upon Vauxhall Walk.”
“Don’t be gloomy, William,” the young man answered. “If that wasn’t the best day’s work I’ve ever done for myself, I’m a Dutchman.”

All that morning and afternoon, Graham Coulton searched carefully for the missing treasure that Mr Tynan assured him had never been found. Youth is confident and full of its own opinions. This new explorer was certain he would succeed where others had failed. He found a locked door on the second floor but paid it little attention for the moment. He thought anything hidden was more likely to be downstairs than upstairs. Late into the evening, he searched the kitchen, the cellars and the many old-fashioned cupboards in the basement.

It was nearly eleven. He was searching among the empty storage compartments of a wine cellar as large as a family burial vault when he suddenly felt cold air rush against his back. As he moved, his candle went out. At the very instant he was left in darkness, he saw a woman standing in the doorway who resembled the one that had haunted his dreams the night before.
He rushed forward with his hands stretched out to seize her, but grasped only air. He relit his candle and carefully searched the basement, first closing off its connection with the ground floor.
All in vain. He found no trace of a living creature. No window was open; no door was unbolted.
“It’s very strange,” he thought. After securely fastening the door at the top of the staircase, he searched the entire upper part of the house, apart from the locked room already mentioned.
“I must get that key tomorrow,” he decided. He stood gloomily with his back to the fire, his eyes wandering round the drawing room, where he had once again settled himself.

As the thought passed through his mind, he saw a woman standing in the open doorway. Her white hair was dishevelled, and her poor clothes were ragged and dirty. She raised a hand and shook it threateningly at him. Then, just as he darted towards her, something astonishing happened.
A second female figure glided from behind the great mirror. At the sight of her, the first turned and fled, shrieking piercingly as the other chased her from floor to floor.
Almost sick with terror, Graham Coulton watched the dreadful pair flee upstairs, past the locked room, to the top of the house.
It took him a few minutes to regain his composure. When he did, he searched the upper rooms and found them completely empty.

Before lying down in front of the fire that night, he carefully locked and bolted the drawing-room door. Before doing anything else, he dragged the heavy bench across it, so that even if the lock were forced, no one could enter without making a great deal of noise.

He lay awake for some time, then fell into a deep sleep. Suddenly a sound woke him, as though something was scuffling stealthily behind the wooden wall panels. He propped himself on one elbow and listened. To his alarm, across the hearth sat the same woman he had seen in his dreams, mourning over her gold.

The fire was not quite out. At that moment, it sent up one last tongue of flame. In that brief light, he saw the figure press a ghostly finger to her lips. Her turned head and the way she held herself suggested she was listening.

He listened too. Indeed, he was too frightened to do anything else. The sounds that had woken him grew clearer: a stealthy rustling coming nearer and nearer, upwards and upwards, it seemed, behind the wall panels.

“It’s rats,” the young man thought, although his teeth were almost chattering with fear. A moment later, something changed his mind: the gleam of a candle or lamp through a crack in the panelling. He tried to get up and struggled to shout, but could do neither. Sinking back, he remembered nothing more until he woke to the grey light of early morning slipping through a shutter he had left partly open.

After a breakfast he barely touched, Graham Coulton spent hours sitting by the fire and thinking. He had examined the house long and carefully that morning, and was still sitting there well after William left him at midday. At last, apparently reaching a decision, he put on the hat he had bought and went out.
When he returned, the evening shadows were deepening. But the pavements were crowded with people buying provisions. It was Christmas Eve, and everyone with money seemed determined to shop.

The old house was terribly dreary inside that night. Graham could feel the ghostly figure wandering mournfully through its empty rooms. When he turned his back, he knew she was flitting from the mirror to the fire, from the fire to the mirror. But he was no longer afraid of her. He was much more afraid of another matter he had taken in hand that day.
The horror of the silent house grew stronger and stronger. In the dead stillness stretching from attic to cellar, he could hear his own heart beating.

At last William arrived. Graham said nothing of what was on his mind. He talked cheerfully and hopefully enough, wondering where his father would think he had gone and hoping Mr Tynan might send him some Christmas pudding. Then William said it was time to leave. When Mr Coulton went downstairs with him to the front door, William remarked that the key was not in it.
“No,” Graham answered, “I took it out today to oil it.”
“It needed oiling,” William agreed. “It was terribly stiff.” Having stated that obvious fact, he left.

Very slowly, the young man went back to the drawing room. He paused only to lock its door from the outside. Then he took off his boots and climbed to the top of the house. Entering the front attic, he waited patiently in darkness and silence.

A long time passed—or so it seemed to him—before he heard the sound that had woken him the night before: a stealthy rustling. Then came a rush of cold air, then cautious footsteps, then the quiet opening of a door below.

The action took less time than the telling. In an instant, the young man was on the landing, closing a section of wall panelling that stood open. He crept noiselessly back to the attic window, unlatched it, and sounded a rattle that echoed far and near through the deserted streets. Then he rushed downstairs and met a man who darted past him towards the landing above. Finding his escape blocked, the man ran back down to find Graham struggling desperately with his companion.

“Stick the knife in him—come on!” he said savagely. The next instant, Graham felt something like a hot iron pass through his shoulder. Then he heard a thud as one of the men tripped in his headlong escape and fell from the top of the stairs to the bottom.
At the same moment came a crash as though the house were collapsing. Faint, sick and bleeding, young Coulton lay unconscious on the threshold of the room where Miss Tynan had been murdered.
When he came to, he was in the dining room, and a doctor was examining his wound.
A policeman stood stiffly on guard near the door. The hall was full of people. All the wretched people and vagrants who filled the streets at that hour were crowding inside to see what had happened.
Through their midst, two men were being taken to the police station. One lay on a stretcher with a dreadful head injury. The other was handcuffed and uttering terrible curses as he went.
After a while, the house was cleared of the rabble, the police took control of it, and someone sent for Mr Tynan.
“What was that dreadful noise?” Graham asked weakly. He was now sitting on the floor with his back against the wall.
“I don’t know. Was there a noise?” Mr Tynan asked, believing he was humouring the young man’s imagination.
“Yes. In the drawing room, I think. The key’s in my pocket.”
Still humouring the wounded boy, Mr Tynan took the key and ran upstairs.

What a sight met him when he unlocked the door! The mirror had fallen and lay across the floor in a thousand pieces. Its weight had brought down the table beneath it, shattering the marble top as well. But that was not what held his attention.
Hundreds—thousands—of gold coins lay scattered about. An opening behind the mirror held boxes filled with securities, deeds and bonds: the possessions that had cost his sister her life.
“Well, Graham, what do you want?” Admiral Coulton asked that evening when his eldest son appeared before him, looking rather pale but otherwise unchanged.

“Nothing,” he answered, “except to ask your forgiveness. William has told me the whole story, which I never knew before. If you’ll let me, I’ll try to make up for the trouble you’ve had. I’m provided for,” he went on with a nervous laugh. “I’ve made my fortune since I left you—and another man’s as well.”
“I think you’ve lost your senses,” the Admiral said sharply.
“No, sir, I’ve found them,” came the answer. “I intend to try to make something better of my life than I ever would have if I hadn’t gone to the Old House in Vauxhall Walk.”
“Vauxhall Walk? What is the boy talking about?”
“I’ll tell you, sir, if I may sit down,” Graham Coulton answered. Then he told his story.
